description: Christian views on family planning, divorce and remarriage, gender equality, and opposition to gender prejudice.
content_html:
Family Planning and Contraception

Christian views on contraception vary significantly across denominations. The Catholic Church’s position is stated in Humanae Vitae (1968, Pope Paul VI): artificial contraception is forbidden because every act of sex must remain open to both its unitive and procreative dimensions. The Catholic Church permits natural family planning (NFP), which works with the body’s natural fertility cycles, because this does not artificially remove the procreative potential from any given act.

Most Protestant denominations — including the Church of England, Baptist, Methodist and Reformed churches — accept artificial contraception as a morally acceptable way to plan a family responsibly. They argue that responsible stewardship of existing relationships and resources, care for existing children, and the wellbeing of the mother are all legitimate moral considerations. From the perspective of situation ethics (Joseph Fletcher, 1966), the most loving decision in each case should determine the choice — and for many couples this will mean using contraception. Humanists and atheists generally regard contraception as a matter of personal autonomy and responsible reproductive decision-making.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae (Pope Paul VI, 1968) forbids artificial contraception — every act of sex must remain open to life. Most Protestant churches accept artificial contraception as responsible family planning. This is a significant divergence within Christianity. The named contrast in the spec is explicitly between “some Protestant Churches” and the Catholic Church.

Divorce and Remarriage

Matthew 19:1–12 records Jesus being questioned by the Pharisees about divorce. Jesus quotes Genesis (“the two will become one flesh”) and states that divorce was only permitted by Moses “because of the hardness of your hearts.” He adds that anyone who divorces and remarries, except for sexual immorality, commits adultery. This passage has shaped Christian teaching on divorce for centuries, though it has been interpreted in very different ways.

The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved (Catechism 2382–2386). Divorce in the civil sense may be permitted to protect legal and financial rights but does not dissolve the marriage in God’s eyes. Remarriage after divorce, without an annulment, is considered adultery. Most Protestant denominations take a more permissive view, allowing divorce and remarriage in cases of irretrievable breakdown, citing compassion and the pastoral need to support people in new life situations. From the perspective of situation ethics, the most loving course of action for a couple in a broken marriage may well be separation and the freedom to begin again. Non-religious people generally regard divorce as a practical solution to a failed relationship with no special moral significance.

The key divergence is between the Catholic insistence on the indissolubility of valid sacramental marriage and the Protestant emphasis on pastoral compassion and the possibility of new beginnings. Catholics point to Matthew 19 and the teaching of Jesus as prohibitive; Protestants also use Matthew 19 but argue that the “except for sexual immorality” clause shows Jesus allowed some exceptions, and that the Church should extend this to other cases of irretrievable breakdown. Some Anglican churches (Church of England) allow remarriage in church at the discretion of the priest; others do not. Orthodox Christianity also permits remarriage after divorce, with a penitential rite. The honest answer in the exam is that there is no single “Christian” view on divorce.

Gender Equality in the Family

Christians believe men and women are created equal in the image of God (Genesis 1–3). The creation accounts in Genesis present both male and female as equally bearing the divine image and equally given dominion over creation. This foundational equality is developed by Paul in Ephesians 5:21–30, which speaks of mutual submission between spouses — “submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” — before giving more specific guidance on the roles of husband and wife. The most important verse for gender equality is Galatians 3:28: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

However, Ephesians 5:21–30 has been interpreted differently across denominations. Conservative Christians argue that Paul’s instruction that husbands are the “head” of the household reflects a God-ordained order, though both spouses are equally loved and valued. Liberal and egalitarian Christians argue that “headship” means servant leadership rather than domination, and that in practice fully equal partnerships reflect the spirit of “mutual submission.”

Key Fact

Galatians 3:23–29: “There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This is the foundational Pauline text for Christian equality. It argues that in Christ, social distinctions (gender, ethnicity, social status) have no ultimate significance — all are equally valuable before God.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

Christianity opposes gender prejudice as inconsistent with the fundamental Christian belief in human dignity. Galatians 3:23–29 is the primary theological foundation: if all are equally valuable in Christ, then treating someone differently because of their gender is a form of injustice that contradicts the gospel. Most denominations formally oppose gender discrimination in all its forms — in employment, in relationships, and in the family.

The most contested area is the role of women in the Church. The Church of England ordained its first female priests in 1994 and its first female bishops in 2015. Many Baptist, Methodist and URC churches have ordained women for decades longer. The Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests, arguing this reflects the example and intention of Jesus. This divergence is one of the most visible examples of how the same biblical texts can be interpreted to reach different practical conclusions about gender roles.

Joseph Fletcher’s situation ethics (1966) argues that love is the only absolute — all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden by the most loving course of action. Applied to gender equality: if any rule or practice restricts women from using their gifts or diminishes their dignity, situation ethics would argue that the loving action is to remove that restriction. Applied to divorce: if remaining in a harmful or loveless marriage causes more suffering than leaving, the loving action is separation and the freedom to begin again. Fletcher was himself a Christian theologian, and his theory has been used by liberal Christians to argue for both gender equality in ministry and compassion in divorce.
exam_tip_html: For 5-mark source questions, use Matthew 19:1–12 for divorce (Jesus on marriage and divorce), Galatians 3:23–29 for gender equality (“neither male nor female”), and Genesis 1–3 for creation equality. The key named sources in the spec are Humanae Vitae (contraception) and Matthew 19. For the 12-mark Discuss on gender equality or divorce, show genuine understanding of why conservative and liberal Christians reach different conclusions from the same Bible — this is what “divergent views” means and what examiners are looking for. Don’t just say “some Christians believe X, others believe Y” without saying which texts each side uses. SPaG: Galatians, Ephesians, Humanae Vitae, situation ethics.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • On contraception, the Catholic Church forbids artificial methods (Humanae Vitae, 1968) while most Protestant churches accept them as responsible family planning. Situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) supports the most loving decision in each case.
  • Matthew 19:1–12 records Jesus teaching against divorce. Catholics do not recognise civil divorce of a sacramental marriage; most Protestant denominations permit divorce and remarriage under certain circumstances.
  • Galatians 3:23–29 (“neither male nor female”) is the foundational Christian text for gender equality. Divergence exists over the role of women in Church leadership — most Protestant denominations ordain women; the Catholic and Orthodox churches do not.

practice_questions.text: Outline three divergent Christian views about contraception.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: the Catholic Church forbids artificial contraception (Humanae Vitae) (1); most Protestant churches accept artificial contraception as responsible family planning (1); natural family planning is accepted by the Catholic Church as it works with the body's natural cycles (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian teaching about divorce and remarriage from Matthew 19:1-12.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Jesus was asked by the Pharisees about divorce (1); he quoted Genesis and said divorce was only permitted 'because of the hardness of your hearts' (1); he stated that remarriage after divorce (except for sexual immorality) is adultery — establishing a strong presumption against divorce (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe men and women are equal.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Genesis 1-3 records both male and female as created in the image of God (imago Dei), implying equal dignity and worth before their Creator (2); Galatians 3:23-29 explicitly states 'there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' — social distinctions have no ultimate significance in the sight of God (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about divorce, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catholics hold that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved — Catechism 2382-2386 teaches that civil divorce does not end the marriage before God, so remarriage without annulment is adultery (2); most Protestant denominations permit divorce and remarriage in cases of irretrievable breakdown, citing pastoral compassion and the 'except for sexual immorality' clause in Matthew 19:1-12 as showing Jesus allowed some exceptions (2); source credit for Matthew 19:1-12 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Christians should fully accept women in all leadership roles in the Church.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Case for: Galatians 3:23-29 ('neither male nor female'); most Protestant denominations have ordained women; Church of England ordained female bishops since 2015. Case against: Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women, citing Jesus's choice of male apostles as a permanent theological intention not a cultural accident. Evaluate: which hermeneutical principle — equality in Christ or the example of Jesus — should carry more weight? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: ordination, Galatians, Ephesians.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which situation ethics differs from Catholic teaching on contraception and divorce, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) holds that no rule is absolute and the most loving action in each situation should guide decisions — so a couple facing hardship may choose contraception as the loving choice, whereas Humanae Vitae (1968) treats the ban on artificial contraception as an absolute rule (2); on divorce, situation ethics would argue that ending a harmful marriage is the most loving option for all involved, whereas the Catholic Church (CCC 2382-2386) does not recognise the dissolution of a sacramental marriage (2); source credit for Humanae Vitae or Matthew 19:1-12 named explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Galatians 3:23-29 say about gender equality?
options: Men and women have different but complementary roles in the Church
There is neither male nor female — all are one in Christ Jesus
Women should not speak in church
Gender equality is only applicable to family life, not to ministry

knowledge_checks.q: What does Matthew 19:1-12 say about why Moses permitted divorce?
options: Because God commanded it in the Law
Because of the hardness of people's hearts
Because marriage was not yet a religious institution
Because women had no legal rights at that time

knowledge_checks.q: Most Protestant denominations _____ artificial contraception as responsible family planning, unlike the Catholic Church.
Ephesians 5:21-30 begins with 'submit to one another out of _____ for Christ' — emphasising mutual submission.
Match each source to its Christian teaching on gender or family:
right: Neither male nor female — all one in Christ
Jesus teaches against divorce — 'what God has joined together'
Artificial contraception forbidden — Pope Paul VI

flashcard_questions.q: What does Galatians 3:23-29 say about gender?
flashcard_questions.a: 'There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' — foundational text for Christian gender equality.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Matthew 19:1-12 say about divorce?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus quotes Genesis and says divorce was only permitted 'because of the hardness of your hearts' — a strong presumption against it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Humanae Vitae and what does it teach?
flashcard_questions.a: A 1968 encyclical by Pope Paul VI — artificial contraception is forbidden because every act of sex must remain open to life.

flashcard_questions.q: How do most Protestant churches differ from the Catholic Church on contraception?
flashcard_questions.a: Most Protestant churches accept artificial contraception as responsible family planning.

flashcard_questions.q: What is situation ethics, and who developed it?
flashcard_questions.a: Joseph Fletcher's 1966 theory that the most loving action in each situation should guide moral decisions — no rule is absolute.

flashcard_questions.q: What do Genesis 1-3 and Galatians 3:28 together establish about gender?
flashcard_questions.a: Both male and female bear the image of God (Genesis) and are equally one in Christ (Galatians) — foundational equality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Catholic Church's position on divorce of a sacramental marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: It cannot be dissolved — civil divorce does not end the marriage before God (CCC 2382-2386).

flashcard_questions.q: What happened in the Church of England regarding women's ordination?
flashcard_questions.a: First female priests in 1994; first female bishops in 2015 — significant development in gender equality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the conservative Christian argument against women's ordination?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus chose only male apostles — Catholics and Orthodox argue this is a permanent theological intention.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Ephesians 5:21-30 say about marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ' — mutual submission is the foundational principle, then roles are discussed.

glossary_terms.definition: Methods of preventing pregnancy — a topic of significant divergence among Christian denominations, with Catholics forbidding artificial methods.
A 1968 encyclical by Pope Paul VI reaffirming Catholic opposition to artificial contraception.
The legal dissolution of a marriage — Christian denominations hold varying views from full prohibition (Catholic) to acceptance in exceptional circumstances (Protestant).
Entering a new marriage after a previous marriage has ended through death or divorce.
An ethical theory developed by Joseph Fletcher (Situation Ethics, 1966) holding that the most loving action in each unique situation should guide moral decisions.
Unjust prejudice or unfair treatment on the grounds of a person's gender — opposed by all major Christian denominations.

glossary_terms.term: role of women in the Church
glossary_terms.definition: Whether women can hold leadership roles including ordained ministry — a point of significant divergence: most Protestant denominations ordain women; Catholics and Orthodox do not.

hero_image_caption: A church interior — representing both the unity and diversity of Christian teaching on gender, family and ethics
